chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd, from Yunus, from Hariz, from Zurara who said:

I asked Abu Abdallah (peace be upon him) about the halal and the haram. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'The halal of Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) is halal forever until the Day of Judgment, and his haram is haram forever until the Day of Judgment. There will be nothing else, nor will anything else come.'
And he said: 'Ali (peace be upon him) said: No one introduces a bid'a (religious innovation) except that a sunnah is abandoned by it.'

key_terms.الْحَرَامِ: haram — what is divinely forbidden; the Prophet's prohibitions remain permanently binding with no possibility of abrogation
key_terms.الْحَلَالِ: halal — what is divinely permitted; here, the totality of what the Prophet (SAWW) declared lawful, binding until the Day of Judgment
key_terms.بِدْعَةً: bid'a — a religious innovation or addition introduced without sanction from revelation or established prophetic practice
key_terms.سُنَّةً: sunnah — an established prophetic practice; this hadith teaches that bid'a does not merely add to but actively displaces and erases an element of sunnah

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) say about the eternal validity of the halal and haram of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) until the Day of Judgment?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) affirms to his companion Zurara that the Prophet Muhammad's (SAWW) legal determinations of halal and haram are eternal and immutable until the Day of Judgment, categorically excluding any future legal revision. He further transmits a maxim of Imam Ali (peace be upon him) warning that every religious innovation (bid'a) inevitably displaces an established element of prophetic practice (sunnah), underscoring the completeness and finality of the prophetic legacy.
